modes.reason: Proposals integrate diversity concept understanding, strategy investigation and community analysis — instruction should position proposals as the culmination of investigation rather than a separate creative task.

descriptors.title: Emotional self-management
descriptors.description: analyse factors that influence emotional responses and devise strategies to self-manage emotions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have applied strategies to manage emotions and analysed how emotional responses influence interactions (Y5-6). They can apply management strategies and describe their effects on interactions, but have not yet been expected to analyse the range of factors that drive emotional responses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse factors that influence emotional responses and devise strategies to self-manage emotions.

nodes.label: Identifying factors that influence emotional responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify personal, social and cultural factors that influence how individuals respond emotionally to situations, with examples of each factor type.
criteria: Identifies at least one personal, social or cultural factor that influences emotional responses
Gives a specific example of how that factor operates in a situation
nodes.hinge_reason: Strategy devising requires students to have identified the specific factors their strategies need to address — generic strategies not connected to specific influences are not responsive to the descriptor's demand for analysis-driven devising.

width.minimum: Identify at least one factor (personal, social or cultural) that influences emotional responses and give a specific example of how it operates.
width.typical: Identify personal, social and cultural factors across a range of situations; describe how each factor type can intensify, moderate or shape the nature of emotional responses; examine how context interacts with these factors.
wider: Investigate how cultural backgrounds shape emotional expression and management norms, examining how different cultural expectations create different 'rules' for emotional response in the same situation

Explore how social media and digital environments create distinctive emotional pressures for young people, identifying what factors make online emotional responses particularly intense or difficult to manage

modes.reason: Build a systematic factor identification framework (personal/social/cultural) and model applying it to a specific situation. Students should be able to use the framework independently before they attempt strategy devising.

nodes.label: Analysing emotional responses in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how specific factors produce specific emotional responses in given situations and evaluate the potential impact of those responses on others.
criteria: Analyses at least one factor that produced an emotional response in a specific situation
Identifies at least one potential impact of that emotional response on others

width.minimum: Analyse one situation where specific factors produced an emotional response and describe one potential impact of that response on others.
width.typical: Analyse emotional responses across multiple situations; practise perspective-taking and empathy to understand how different people experience the same situation differently; recognise and interpret responses to stressful situations.
wider: Explore different viewpoints and practise empathy by considering alternative ways to respond in a variety of situations, examining how the same situation produces different emotional responses for different people based on their personal, social or cultural factors
Analyse emotional responses to stressful situations encountered specifically in digital and online environments, examining how these differ from face-to-face responses and why

modes.reason: Emotional analysis is enriched by perspective diversity — encountering how the same situation produces different responses for different people (due to different personal, social, cultural factors) deepens analytical understanding.

nodes.label: Devising self-management strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can devise strategies to self-manage emotional responses that are specifically responsive to identified influencing factors, and evaluate their likely effectiveness.
criteria: Devises at least one strategy for self-managing an emotional response in a specific situation
Explains why the strategy addresses the factors influencing that response
Considers how the strategy prevents or limits negative impact on others

width.minimum: Devise at least one strategy for self-managing an emotional response in a specific situation and give a reason why it would be effective.
width.typical: Devise a range of self-management strategies responsive to different factor types and situations; evaluate which strategies are most appropriate for specific emotional contexts; ensure proposed strategies prevent negative impact on others.
wider: Recognise and interpret emotional responses to stressful situations and devise strategies that ensure those responses don't negatively impact others, practising strategies in simulated or role-play contexts
Design a personal emotional self-management toolkit that includes strategies for both in-person and digital/online contexts, with justification for each strategy's relevance

modes.reason: Devising strategies integrates factor analysis, emotional understanding and practical planning — the strategies produced should be visibly connected to the analysis completed in prior nodes, not generated independently.

descriptors.title: Assertive consent communication
descriptors.description: explain and apply skills and strategies to communicate assertively and respectfully when seeking, giving or denying consent
descriptors.knowledge: Students have described strategies for seeking, giving or denying consent and rehearsed how to communicate their intentions effectively and respectfully (Y5-6). They have practised communication strategies in basic scenarios but have not yet been expected to explain the rationale behind assertive communication or apply it across more complex relationship and digital contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain and apply skills and strategies to communicate assertively and respectfully when seeking, giving or denying consent.

nodes.label: Understanding consent and assertive communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what consent means in different relationship types and describe what assertive, respectful communication looks like compared to passive or aggressive communication.
criteria: Explains what consent means in at least one relationship context
Describes at least one characteristic of assertive communication that distinguishes it from passive or aggressive communication
nodes.hinge_reason: Application of assertive consent communication requires students to know what they are trying to achieve — students who cannot distinguish assertive from passive or aggressive communication will not be able to recognise or practise the specific communication skills the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Explain what consent means in at least one relationship context and describe one characteristic of assertive (as distinct from aggressive or passive) communication.
width.typical: Explain consent across different relationship types (friendships, romantic/sexual relationships, online interactions); describe the characteristics of assertive communication; explain why assertiveness protects both parties in a consent interaction.
wider: Examine the nature of consent in different types of relationships — including online and digital contexts — and identify what makes consent communication more complex in each
Investigate how online and social protocols differ from face-to-face consent communication, and what strategies protect wellbeing in online interactions

modes.reason: Use clear conceptual differentiation: assertive (clear, respectful, self-respecting), passive (unclear, deferring), aggressive (disrespectful, coercive). Apply the distinction to consent scenarios before practising the skill.

nodes.label: Exploring skills and strategies for consent communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain specific skills and strategies for seeking, giving and denying consent assertively and respectfully, including in online contexts.
criteria: Identifies at least one skill or strategy for assertive consent communication
Explains why the skill or strategy is effective for seeking, giving or denying consent

width.minimum: Identify at least one skill or strategy for communicating assertively when seeking, giving or denying consent and explain why it is effective.
width.typical: Explore and refine a range of skills and strategies for assertive consent communication across in-person and online contexts; recognise and respond to harmful online content (grooming, image-based abuse); explain how digital communication creates additional challenges for consent.
wider: Explore strategies for recognising and responding to online content that may be harmful — such as grooming or image-based abuse — and practise communicating needs or concerns assertively in these situations
Examine how power imbalances, group pressure and digital contexts complicate consent communication, and identify strategies that remain effective in these more challenging conditions

modes.reason: Students need multiple strategies across multiple contexts — no single strategy works in all consent situations. Building a repertoire that spans in-person and online contexts is essential before application.

nodes.label: Applying consent communication skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply skills and strategies for assertive, respectful consent communication in a range of scenarios, demonstrating the ability to seek, give and deny consent.
criteria: Applies at least one assertive consent communication strategy in a practice scenario
Demonstrates the ability to seek, give or deny consent in the scenario
Evaluates the effectiveness of the strategy used

width.minimum: Apply at least one assertive consent communication strategy in a practice scenario involving seeking, giving or denying consent.
width.typical: Apply consent communication skills across multiple scenarios including face-to-face and online/digital contexts; practise seeking, giving and denying consent assertively; evaluate the effectiveness of strategies used in each scenario.
wider: Examine and practise strategies for assertive consent communication in situations where consent is complicated by power imbalances or digital dynamics

Design and role-play scenarios that require assertive consent communication in a range of realistic relationship and digital contexts, reflecting on what made each scenario challenging and what strategies were most effective

modes.reason: Assertive communication is a practiced skill — role-play and scenario practice need to be repeated across varied scenarios to build the confidence and habit that enables real-world application.

descriptors.title: Protective behaviours and community resources
descriptors.description: refine protective behaviours and evaluate community resources to seek help for themselves and others
descriptors.knowledge: Students have analysed and rehearsed protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies in online and offline situations (Y5-6). They have rehearsed protective behaviours but have not yet been expected to refine them through evaluation or to evaluate the quality and suitability of community resources.
descriptors.endpoint: Students refine protective behaviours and evaluate community resources to seek help for themselves and others.

nodes.label: Identifying protective behaviours and when they apply
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a range of protective behaviours appropriate to different risk or help-seeking scenarios and explain the reasoning behind each.
criteria: Identifies at least two protective behaviours
Explains the reasoning behind each behaviour in a specific scenario

width.minimum: Identify at least two protective behaviours and explain the reasoning behind each in a specific scenario.
width.typical: Identify protective behaviours across a range of scenarios (mental health, online abuse, substance use, sexual health, bullying); explain why each behaviour protects safety or wellbeing in its specific context; distinguish proactive from reactive protective behaviours.
wider: Explore help-seeking scenarios young people may encounter — including situations linked to substance use, mental health, sexual health, safety and risk-taking — and identify which protective behaviours are most relevant to each

Investigate how emotions, gender norms and cultural expectations can affect a person's willingness to apply protective behaviours or seek help, and what this means for designing effective protective strategies

modes.reason: Protective behaviour application depends on having a range of behaviours available — students who only know one or two protective strategies will be unable to respond appropriately to diverse scenarios.

nodes.label: Evaluating community resources for help-seeking
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and evaluate community resources available for help-seeking in a range of scenarios, assessing their accessibility, relevance and quality.
criteria: Identifies at least one community resource available for help-seeking in a named scenario
Evaluates the resource against at least one criterion (accessibility, reliability or relevance)
nodes.hinge_reason: Refining protective behaviours and evaluating resources are the twin demands of this descriptor — students who cannot evaluate resource quality cannot make informed help-seeking decisions for themselves or others. This evaluation capability is what separates knowing resources exist from being able to use them effectively.

width.minimum: Identify at least one community resource available for help-seeking in a specific scenario and give one reason for or against using it.
width.typical: Identify and evaluate resources across multiple domains (mental health, online safety, substance use, sexual health); assess accessibility, reliability and relevance for different scenarios; examine how support services like Kidshelpline and eSafety Commissioner operate.
wider: Analyse how online support services (Kidshelpline, eSafety Commissioner) are designed and evaluate their effectiveness for different types of situations young people encounter
Examine how gender norms and cultural expectations create barriers to help-seeking for different groups and evaluate which resources are designed to address these barriers

modes.reason: Provide explicit evaluation criteria (accessibility, relevance, reliability, appropriateness for specific scenarios) before expecting evaluation judgements. Without criteria, resource evaluation defaults to surface-level familiarity.

nodes.label: Refining protective behaviours through scenario practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply and refine protective behaviours across a range of help-seeking scenarios, adjusting their approach based on the specific context and available resources.
criteria: Applies protective behaviours in at least one scenario
Identifies at least one way to refine the approach for the specific context
Connects at least one protective behaviour to a specific community resource that would support it

width.minimum: Apply protective behaviours in at least one scenario and describe one way they refined their approach based on the specific context.
width.typical: Apply and refine protective behaviours across multiple scenario types; explain how bystanders play a role in ensuring safety; practise strategies for managing online abuse, substance pressure and mental health crises; connect protective behaviours to specific community resources.
wider: Explore strategies for dealing with online abuse and bullying when there is an imbalance of power — including grooming and image-based abuse — and practise reporting situations to appropriate authorities and through online tools
Collaborate with peers to suggest strategies for scenarios where a friend is being encouraged to use a substance, evaluating which strategies are most likely to be effective in a real peer context

modes.reason: Protective behaviour refinement requires repeated scenario practice — one rehearsal does not build the reliable, habitual responses that protective behaviour depends on in real situations.
Refined protective behaviours integrate knowledge of scenarios, resource evaluation and practical strategy — connecting resources to behaviours is essential so students can act, not just plan.

descriptors.title: Media influence on health
descriptors.description: investigate how media and influential people impact attitudes, beliefs, decisions and behaviours in relation to health, safety, relationships and wellbeing
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated different sources and types of health information and how these apply to health choices (Y5-6). They can identify and apply health information but have not yet been expected to investigate the mechanisms by which media and influential figures shape attitudes and beliefs — not just inform decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how media and influential people impact attitudes, beliefs, decisions and behaviours in relation to health, safety, relationships and wellbeing.

nodes.label: Understanding how media shapes health attitudes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how different types of media sources and influential people can shape attitudes and beliefs about health, safety, relationships and wellbeing — beyond just providing information.
criteria: Identifies at least one media source and explains how it operates as a shaper of attitudes or beliefs
Distinguishes between providing information and shaping attitudes in at least one example
nodes.hinge_reason: The descriptor asks students to investigate impact on attitudes, beliefs, decisions and behaviours — not just to evaluate source credibility. Students who only understand media as information provision cannot investigate attitudinal and behavioural influence, which is the primary focus of this descriptor.

width.minimum: Identify one media source and explain one way it shapes attitudes or beliefs about health (not just provides information about it).
width.typical: Explain how different source types (news, bloggers, influencers, social media advertising) operate differently as attitude and belief shapers; distinguish between informing, persuading and normalising as media mechanisms; connect media exposure to attitude formation across multiple health domains.
wider: Analyse how social media algorithms shape what health information young people see, and evaluate what media literacy strategies help students navigate this curated environment
Explore how messages related to food are portrayed in media and how this shapes decision-making about health and wellbeing, examining both explicit messaging and normalisation through representation

modes.reason: Distinguish between media as information source and media as attitude/belief shaper. Explicitly model the mechanism: exposure → normalisation → attitude → behaviour. Without this distinction, students evaluate credibility but do not investigate influence.

nodes.label: Analysing credibility and investigating influence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the credibility, validity and relevance of health messages from media and influential people, and explain how these messages may influence health-related attitudes, beliefs and decisions.
criteria: Analyses at least one health message from a media source using credibility, validity or relevance as a criterion
Explains how the message might influence attitudes, beliefs or decisions

width.minimum: Analyse the credibility of one health message from a media source and explain one way it might influence attitudes or decisions.
width.typical: Analyse credibility, validity and relevance across a range of source types; investigate how sexual relationship messages, body image messages and health information are constructed across different media forms; apply credible information to health-related decisions.
wider: Explore health campaigns targeting First Nations Australian young people (Deadly Choices, Don't Make Smokes Your Story, Yarn Safe) and analyse the messages, strategies and cultural framing used to promote health
Analyse how messages related to sexual relationships are portrayed in different media forms and evaluate how they may influence the way people act within relationships

modes.reason: Credibility analysis and influence investigation across multiple health domains (food, sexual health, body image, mental health) prevents students from developing a single-domain framework that does not generalise.

nodes.label: Applying critical media literacy to health decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply critical analysis of media health messages to inform their own health-related decisions and evaluate the impact of media influence on themselves and others.
criteria: Applies analysis of a media health message to inform or evaluate a health-related decision
Evaluates at least one way media influence has affected health attitudes, beliefs or behaviours in a specific context

width.minimum: Apply an analysis of a media health message to inform at least one health-related decision or evaluate one way media has influenced their own or others' health attitudes.
width.typical: Apply credibility analysis and influence understanding to health decisions across multiple domains; evaluate the impact of media influence on health attitudes and behaviours; explore how to access reliable health information sources for specific health questions.
wider: Evaluate the accessibility and reliability of health information sources that target young people in relation to their health, wellbeing, body, sexuality and relationships — building a personal framework for evaluating sources
Investigate how algorithmic curation of health content creates echo chambers and evaluate strategies for diversifying the health information young people encounter

modes.reason: Applied media literacy integrates source analysis, influence mechanism understanding and personal decision-making — the application should explicitly connect the analytical skills built in prior nodes to concrete health decision contexts.

descriptors.title: Health strategies and resources
descriptors.description: plan and implement strategies, using health resources, to enhance their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing
descriptors.knowledge: Students have analysed how behaviours influence the health, safety, relationships and wellbeing of individuals and communities (Y5-6). They can analyse behavioural influence but have not yet been expected to plan and implement strategies using specific health resources to produce health enhancement outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan and implement strategies using health resources to enhance their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing.

nodes.label: Identifying health needs and relevant resources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific health, safety or wellbeing needs relevant to themselves or their peer group and locate health resources relevant to addressing those needs.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific health, safety or wellbeing need
Locates at least one health resource relevant to addressing that need

width.minimum: Identify at least one health, safety or wellbeing need and locate at least one health resource relevant to addressing it.
width.typical: Identify health needs across multiple domains (nutrition, physical activity, mental health, digital wellbeing, sexual health, preventive practices); locate and assess relevant resources from multiple sources; evaluate resource quality and relevance.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians have developed complete diets meeting nutritional requirements and used food for medicinal purposes, and examine how this knowledge connects to understanding health resources more broadly

Research how different cultural traditions value mind-body-spirit connections to health (e.g. Dadirri from First Nations communities of the Daly River region; yoga and meditation from the Asian region) and evaluate their relevance as health resources

modes.reason: Health resource identification across multiple domains builds the breadth students need to plan strategies that address the full scope of the descriptor (health, safety, relationships, wellbeing).

nodes.label: Planning health enhancement strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a strategy to enhance health, safety or wellbeing for themselves or others, incorporating relevant health resources and realistic implementation steps.
criteria: Plans a strategy to enhance health, safety or wellbeing
Incorporates at least one health resource in the plan
Identifies at least one realistic implementation step
nodes.hinge_reason: Implementation quality depends on planning quality — students who produce vague or resource-disconnected plans will be unable to implement strategically and will not achieve the enhancement outcomes the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Plan one strategy to enhance health, safety or wellbeing that incorporates at least one health resource and identifies at least one implementation step.
width.typical: Plan strategies across multiple health domains; use health guidelines (e.g. Australian Guide to Healthy Eating, physical activity guidelines) to inform plans; ensure plans are realistic and achievable; design plans for both personal and others-focused outcomes.
wider: Design a preventive health promotion plan targeting a health practice relevant to young people, drawing on research evidence and community health resources

Investigate food-serving recommendations from the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and design a practical guide to help students make healthier choices in a specific real-world context (e.g. school canteen)

modes.reason: Scaffold planning with a consistent structure: identify the need, identify the resource, design the strategy, predict the outcome, identify implementation steps. Without structure, plans tend to be aspirational without being actionable.

nodes.label: Implementing and evaluating strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can implement a health enhancement strategy and evaluate its impact on their own or others' health, safety, relationships or wellbeing.
criteria: Implements a planned health enhancement strategy
Evaluates at least one impact of the strategy on health, safety, relationships or wellbeing
Identifies at least one way the strategy could be refined based on the evaluation

width.minimum: Implement one health enhancement strategy and describe at least one observed or expected impact on health, safety, relationships or wellbeing.
width.typical: Implement and evaluate strategies across multiple health domains; evaluate nutritional value, sustainability and other criteria relevant to specific strategies; assess impact on health outcomes; propose adjustments based on evaluation findings.
wider: Implement health promotion activities targeting preventive health practices for young people and evaluate their impact on attitudes or behaviours within a school or community context
Investigate tools and design routines that help regulate digital environment use and ensure healthy patterns — implementing and evaluating the design in their own daily context
Examine how different approaches to promoting positive mental health (mindfulness, relaxation, healthy eating) compare in effectiveness, and develop a personal plan incorporating multiple strategies

modes.reason: Implementation and evaluation integrates needs identification, resource knowledge and planning into action and reflection — instruction should scaffold the full plan-implement-evaluate cycle as a connected process.

descriptors.title: Analyse and enhance performance
descriptors.description: analyse, adapt and refine their own and others' movement skills in a range of challenging movement situations to enhance performance
descriptors.knowledge: Students can demonstrate and explain how movement concepts can be manipulated to improve movement outcomes (AC9HP8M03). At Y9-10 the focus moves to analysis of performance with feedback — using knowledge of results, digital tools, and constructive peer feedback to refine skills in challenging situations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse, adapt and refine their own and others' movement skills in challenging situations, using feedback mechanisms including digital tools to enhance performance.

nodes.label: Analysing movement performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse movement performance — their own and others' — identifying what needs to be refined and why
criteria: Identifies at least two specific aspects of a performance that affect the outcome
Explains why each aspect matters — not just that it is 'good' or 'bad'
Analysis is specific enough to inform a refinement action — generic ('needs to be faster') is insufficient
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot analyse what specifically needs to change in a performance cannot meaningfully adapt or refine it in Node 2 — adaptation and refinement require a prior analytical judgement about what the current performance is producing and what it needs to produce instead.

width.minimum: Observe a movement performance (their own or a peer's) and identify at least two specific aspects that affect the outcome — explain why each matters for performance quality
width.typical: Use knowledge of results feedback to analyse performance with accuracy and control; analyse performances (e.g. swimming, athletics, cross-country) and propose strategies for refining technique; use digital tools to record and analyse timing of movements in relation to teammates, opposition or external stimuli
wider: Use video analysis tools to compare own performance against a reference model — identify specific timing, positioning or technique differences and explain their effect on outcome
Analyse performance changes when equipment is varied (e.g. different bat weight, ball type, resistance) — evaluate which equipment adaptations improve performance and why

Provide constructive performance feedback to a peer using a structured framework (e.g. two specific observations, one improvement focus) — evaluate whether the feedback resulted in a measurable change

modes.reason: Students commonly observe performances and describe what they see without analysing why it matters for performance outcome. The structured reasoning investment is in building the analysis chain: what is the specific movement pattern, what effect does it have on the outcome, what would a refined version look like. Digital tools support this — video allows repeated review that verbal observation cannot match.

nodes.label: Adapting and refining skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adapt and refine movement skills in response to analysis and feedback across challenging movement situations
criteria: Makes a specific adaptation in response to analysis or feedback
Evaluates whether the adaptation improved the performance outcome with reference to observable evidence
Adaptation is connected to the analysis — not a random change

width.minimum: Make one specific adaptation to a movement skill based on analysis; evaluate whether the adaptation improved the performance outcome
width.typical: Adapt and respond to changes in equipment or conditions that increase complexity; provide and act on constructive feedback on group performance of a movement sequence; analyse performances across multiple activity types and refine techniques in response; evaluate effectiveness of adaptations
wider: Refine performance in response to digital feedback across multiple trial repetitions — evaluate which adaptations produced the most significant improvement and why
Adapt movement skills to a novel activity context (e.g. transfer batting technique to a new sport) and evaluate what transferred effectively and what needed further adaptation
Lead a peer refinement session — analyse a group member's performance, provide structured feedback, support the refinement attempt, and evaluate the outcome

modes.reason: Adapting and refining movement skills builds through practice across multiple activity contexts and feedback cycles. A single adaptation attempt is insufficient — students need to develop a repertoire of adaptive responses across different movement challenges, equipment types, and performance contexts. The elaborations explicitly require multiple activity types.

descriptors.title: Create movement strategies
descriptors.description: create and refine movement strategies to achieve successful outcomes across a range of challenging movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse, adapt and refine movement skills in challenging situations to enhance performance (AC9HP10M01), and have previously designed and demonstrated how movement strategies can be manipulated to improve outcomes (AC9HP8M02). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to creating original strategies rather than adapting existing ones.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and refine movement strategies to achieve successful outcomes across challenging movement situations, using self-developed evaluation criteria to assess and adapt strategies.

nodes.label: Creating movement strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create original movement strategies for specific challenging movement situations
criteria: Creates a strategy with a named intended outcome
Explains the reasoning behind at least two strategic choices — not just describes what the strategy involves
Strategy is appropriate to the specific movement situation — not generic
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot create an original strategy with explicit reasoning cannot refine it in Node 2 — refinement requires having a strategy with an intended outcome that can be evaluated against results.

width.minimum: Create one movement strategy for a specific game or movement challenge; explain the intended outcome and the reasoning behind the strategic choices made
width.typical: Create movement strategies that respond to specific situational demands; perform specialised movement skills in situations where rules or conditions have been modified to vary complexity; propose and implement alternative responses to movement situations based on previous performance outcomes
wider: Create a movement strategy for a modified or unfamiliar game — evaluate how well the strategy accounts for the specific constraints and opportunities of the modified rules
Develop a strategic response to a movement situation involving different equipment types — create and compare strategies optimised for each equipment variation
Create a strategy for a collaborative movement challenge (e.g. outdoor adventure activity) that accounts for varying capability levels within the group

modes.reason: Students commonly perform movement strategies without creating them explicitly — acting intuitively without articulating the strategic logic. The investment here is in making the creation process explicit: what is the situation, what outcome am I trying to achieve, what strategic choices does that require, and why. Articulating the creation logic is prerequisite for the evaluation and refinement work in Node 2.

nodes.label: Refining strategies through evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of movement strategies using self-developed criteria and refine them in response
criteria: States at least one self-developed criterion for evaluating the strategy
Evaluates whether the strategy achieved its intended outcome — with specific reference to what happened
Makes at least one concrete refinement connected to the evaluation finding

width.minimum: Evaluate one movement strategy against at least one self-developed criterion; explain what the evaluation revealed and what refinement was made
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of a range of strategies in game situations using personally developed criteria; adapt and refine strategies based on evaluation; suggest how refined strategies can be applied to improve performance across different game or movement situations
wider: Develop a multi-criteria evaluation framework for movement strategy effectiveness; apply it across two or more different game situations and compare results
Review performance data from digital tools (video, timing) to evaluate strategy effectiveness — refine strategy based on data rather than only subjective impression
Evaluate a peer's strategy using their own stated criteria — provide specific feedback on the gap between intended and actual outcomes, and collaboratively refine the strategy

modes.reason: Strategy creation and refinement improves through application across multiple movement situations and evaluation cycles. Students need to develop a repertoire of strategies across different game types and conditions — and a repertoire of evaluation approaches — rather than perfecting a single strategy in one context.

descriptors.title: Apply movement concepts
descriptors.description: apply movement concepts in new or challenging movement situations and analyse the impact each concept has on movement outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and refine movement strategies to achieve successful outcomes in challenging situations (AC9HP10M02), and have previously demonstrated and explained how movement concepts (effort, space, time, objects, people) can be manipulated to improve outcomes (AC9HP8M03). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to applying concepts in new or challenging situations and analysing the impact of each concept.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply movement concepts in new or challenging situations and analyse the impact each concept has on movement outcomes, including force absorption, synchronisation, and space/time modifications.

nodes.label: Applying movement concepts in new situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliberately apply movement concepts in new or challenging movement situations
criteria: Names a specific movement concept and the situation it is being applied in
Explains the intended effect of applying the concept — not just that they used it
Application is in a new or challenging context — not a familiar, well-practised one
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot deliberately apply a movement concept in a new situation cannot analyse its impact in Node 2 — analysis of impact requires first having intentionally varied the concept so that its effect can be observed.

width.minimum: Identify one movement concept (e.g. force, speed, space, time) being applied in a new or challenging situation and explain the intended effect
width.typical: Apply movement concepts in new or challenging situations; experiment with the manipulation of force and speed applied to objects to examine differences in movement paths (e.g. topspin, outswing); create and evaluate group performances demonstrating synchronous and individual movements
wider: Apply the concept of force manipulation to two or more different sports or activities — compare how the same concept operates differently across different equipment types and movement contexts
Investigate how synchronous movement in group performance requires application of multiple concepts simultaneously (time, space, people) — design and evaluate a sequence that demonstrates this
Apply space and time concepts to analyse and describe how performance has improved through modifications — compare individual and team level impacts

modes.reason: Movement concepts applied in a single familiar activity may produce pattern-matching rather than genuine concept understanding. Applying the same concept across multiple new or challenging situations — different sports, different equipment, different group configurations — reveals whether students understand the concept or only recognise it in one context.

nodes.label: Analysing impact of movement concepts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the impact of specific movement concepts on movement outcomes
criteria: Names a specific movement concept and a specific outcome it affected
Analyses the mechanism — how the concept produced that outcome, not just that it did
Analysis is specific enough to inform a coaching or refinement decision

width.minimum: Analyse one movement concept and explain its impact on a specific movement outcome — what changed and why
width.typical: Analyse how force absorption techniques prevent injury across game situations; analyse how space and time modifications improve individual or team performance; evaluate which techniques for absorbing force are most effective for preventing injury in different contexts
wider: Analyse force absorption across a range of game situations — evaluate which techniques are most effective, in which contexts, and why — connect to injury prevention and performance
Analyse how modifying space and time in a team activity changes the nature of the challenge for all participants — evaluate the impact on both performance and inclusion
Conduct a systematic analysis of one movement concept across a personal performance sequence — trace its impact at each phase and propose concept-specific refinements

modes.reason: Students often describe what a movement concept is or how it is used without analysing its impact — they identify that force absorption reduces injury risk without explaining the mechanism (how absorbing force over greater distance or time reduces peak force on joints). The structured reasoning investment is in building the impact chain: concept applied, mechanism, outcome produced.

descriptors.title: Design personalised activity plans
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities designed to enhance health, wellbeing and fitness, and design, apply and evaluate strategies for incorporating these activities into their lives
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design and justify strategies to increase physical activity to achieve health and wellbeing outcomes (AC9HP8M06). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to personalisation — designing, applying and evaluating strategies that incorporate specific physical activities into their own lives, including understanding individual physiological responses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in fitness-enhancing activities, design personalised strategies for incorporating them into their lives, and evaluate those strategies against fitness and wellbeing goals.

nodes.label: Understanding individual physiological responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate their body's responses to physical activity at different intensities and connect these to fitness components
criteria: Names at least two physiological responses observed during activity
Explains what each response indicates about exertion level or fitness demand
Connects at least one response to a specific fitness component (e.g. cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot interpret their own physiological responses to physical activity cannot make evidence-based decisions about activity selection and intensity in their personalised plan (Node 2) — the design requires understanding what the body is signalling during and after activity.

width.minimum: Participate in a physical activity and identify at least two physiological responses (e.g. heart rate, breathing rate, ability to talk, recovery rate); explain what each response indicates
width.typical: Participate in a range of physical activities and evaluate individual responses including heart rate, breathing rate, ability to talk and recovery rate; perform activities designed to improve fitness and analyse how each improves specific fitness components
wider: Investigate target training heart-rate zones for different individuals — explain how these zones are measured, how they relate to fitness level, and how they should inform activity selection for different health goals
Compare physiological responses across different activity types at the same perceived effort level — evaluate what this reveals about relative fitness demands
Analyse how individual factors (age, fitness level, health condition) affect physiological responses to the same activity — evaluate what this means for personalised plan design

modes.reason: Students often participate in activities and report physiological responses without interpreting what they mean. The structured reasoning investment is in building the interpretation chain: this response occurred, it indicates this physiological state, this implies this about fitness demand or intensity level, therefore this about activity design. Heart rate zones add a quantitative framework that supports this reasoning.

nodes.label: Designing and evaluating personalised plans
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design, apply and evaluate a personalised strategy for incorporating physical activity into their life
criteria: Plan includes at least one specific, measurable goal
Activity selection is justified with reference to the goal and individual physiological needs
Evaluation addresses whether the goal was achieved and identifies at least one factor that affected adherence or outcome

width.minimum: Design a personalised physical activity plan with at least one realistic goal; apply it for a period and evaluate whether it achieved the goal
width.typical: Set realistic physical activity goals; design, implement and evaluate a personalised program incorporating regular physical activity into weekly routines; justify the selection of activities linked to goals and wellbeing outcomes; use digital tools to design, monitor and adjust the plan
wider: Design a personalised plan that incorporates target heart-rate zones for different workout types — justify intensity choices with reference to fitness goals and physiological evidence
Evaluate a personalised plan across a multi-week implementation — track progress against goals and make documented adjustments; evaluate what factors supported or hindered adherence
Design a personalised plan for a different person (e.g. a family member with different fitness goals) — justify the adaptations made and evaluate what personalisation required

modes.reason: Designing and evaluating personalised plans builds through the cycle of planning, implementing, evaluating, and adjusting. A single design exercise without implementation and evaluation is insufficient — students need experience of the full cycle, including what happens when a plan is harder to adhere to than expected. The digital tools direction supports ongoing monitoring rather than one-off evaluation.

descriptors.title: Health and social outcomes
descriptors.description: participate in physical activities that promote health and social outcomes to design and evaluate participation strategies for themselves and others
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design, apply and evaluate personalised strategies for incorporating physical activity into their lives (AC9HP10M04). At Y9-10 this standard shifts focus from individual fitness planning to the social dimensions of physical activity participation — designing strategies that promote both health and social connection for themselves and others.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in physical activities that promote health and social outcomes, and design and evaluate participation strategies for themselves and others.

nodes.label: Physical activity for social outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and participate in physical activities that promote social outcomes alongside health benefits
criteria: Names a specific physical activity and identifies both a health and a social outcome it promotes
Distinguishes social outcomes (e.g. connection, belonging, inclusion) from health outcomes (e.g. fitness, wellbeing)
Identifies at least one community space or resource where the activity could be pursued

width.minimum: Participate in at least one physical activity with a clear social dimension; identify one health and one social outcome it promotes
width.typical: Participate in physical activities that promote health and social outcomes; identify local natural resources and community spaces where individuals and groups can connect through physical and social activities; investigate community-based campaigns promoting physical activity participation
wider: Investigate how culturally significant physical activities create community connection and belonging — evaluate the social outcomes these activities produce beyond physical health benefits
Identify and visit or research local natural settings for physical activity in the community — evaluate how accessible they are for different groups and what could increase their use
Participate in or investigate a community campaign promoting physical activity — determine the key elements that made it successful and evaluate whether they could be replicated in a school context

modes.reason: Social outcomes from physical activity are highly context-dependent — what builds community connection in one cultural or community setting differs from another. Students need to engage with multiple activity types and community contexts to develop genuine understanding of how physical activity produces social outcomes, not just health ones.

nodes.label: Designing participation strategies for others
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design and evaluate participation strategies for physical activities that promote health and social outcomes for themselves and others
criteria: Designs a strategy for a named target group — not a generic strategy
Strategy promotes both health and social outcomes — addresses both, not only one
Evaluation addresses whether the strategy is realistic and accessible for the target group

width.minimum: Design one strategy for increasing participation in a physical activity with health and social benefits; explain who it is designed for and why it would be effective for that group
width.typical: Create and evaluate proposals to promote use of natural settings for physical activity; design strategies involving family, friends and community in culturally significant physical activities that promote connection and belonging; evaluate participation strategies against health and social outcome goals
wider: Design and evaluate a strategy to involve a specific community group (e.g. elderly residents, culturally and linguistically diverse community members) in a physical activity that promotes health and social connection — justify design choices for that specific group
Create a proposal for a community celebration based around culturally significant physical activities — evaluate how it would promote a sense of belonging for diverse community members
Investigate and evaluate a school-based physical activity participation strategy — identify what elements are working, what barriers exist, and propose specific improvements based on evidence

modes.reason: Students commonly design participation strategies without evaluating whether they will work for the intended audience — designing a strategy for 'everyone' without considering what barriers different groups face. The structured reasoning investment is in making the design decisions explicit: who is this for, what barriers do they face, how does this strategy address those barriers, how will health and social outcomes be achieved.

descriptors.title: Personalised physical activity plans
descriptors.description: design, implement and evaluate personalised plans for improving or maintaining their own or others' physical activity levels to achieve fitness, health and wellbeing outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: Students can participate in activities promoting health and social outcomes and design participation strategies (AC9HP10M05), and have designed and applied personalised activity strategies (AC9HP10M04). This standard extends to explicitly implementing and evaluating multi-goal personalised plans for themselves or others, including using digital tools and heart-rate zone knowledge.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design, implement and evaluate personalised physical activity plans — for themselves or others — to achieve specific fitness, health and wellbeing outcomes.

nodes.label: Designing a personalised plan
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a personalised physical activity plan with justified activity selections linked to specific goals
criteria: Plan includes at least one specific, measurable goal
Each activity selection is justified with reference to the goal and a fitness component
Plan is realistic for the intended person — accounts for their current fitness level and available time
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot design a plan with justified activity selections cannot implement it purposefully or evaluate it meaningfully in Node 2 — implementation without a justified design is just exercise, and evaluation requires a stated intention to evaluate against.

width.minimum: Design a personalised plan with at least two specific activities; justify why each activity was selected based on the goal and individual needs
width.typical: Design a personalised physical activity plan using digital tools; include a timeframe, specific goals, and a variety of activities that meet the needs of different people; justify activity selections linked to physical activity goals and wellbeing outcomes; investigate target heart-rate zones for different people and incorporate into plan design
wider: Design a personalised plan for a different person (e.g. with different fitness levels, age, or health conditions) — justify how the design differs from a plan for yourself and why
Incorporate heart-rate zone calculations into a multi-week plan — justify how each session's intensity is matched to a specific fitness component goal
Use digital planning tools to build a plan that tracks multiple variables (frequency, intensity, duration, type) and includes built-in monitoring and adjustment triggers

modes.reason: Students commonly design plans by listing activities they enjoy without justifying how each activity contributes to the stated goal. The investment is in building the design justification chain: goal → fitness component → activity type → intensity and frequency → how it produces the desired outcome. Heart-rate zone knowledge supports this reasoning quantitatively.

nodes.label: Implementing and evaluating the plan
nodes.checkpoint: Students can implement and evaluate a personalised physical activity plan, making evidence-based adjustments
criteria: Implements the plan for a defined period — not only designs it
Evaluation addresses whether the goal was achieved, with specific evidence
Identifies at least one factor that influenced adherence and explains its effect on outcomes

width.minimum: Implement the plan for a defined period and evaluate whether it achieved its goal; identify one factor that supported and one that hindered adherence
width.typical: Implement and monitor a personalised plan; evaluate against fitness and wellbeing goals; document adjustments made and reasons for them; use digital tools to track activity levels and evaluate progress; justify ongoing activity selections against changing goals or fitness levels
wider: Track implementation across multiple weeks using digital monitoring tools — evaluate patterns in adherence and performance; make documented, justified adjustments to the plan in response to data

Evaluate a personalised plan designed for another person — assess whether the plan met their needs, what worked, what needed adjustment, and what the evaluation reveals about designing effective plans for others
Compare outcomes from two different plan designs (e.g. high frequency/low intensity vs low frequency/high intensity) and evaluate which better achieved the stated goals for this individual

modes.reason: Implementation and evaluation capability develops through repeated plan-implement-evaluate cycles, not a single experience. Students who only evaluate one plan have limited basis for understanding what makes plans effective or how to adjust them. Multiple cycles — including adjusting based on findings — build genuine capability for lifelong physical activity planning.

descriptors.title: Transfer skills to unfamiliar situations
descriptors.description: transfer and adapt skills and strategies from previous experiences to create successful outcomes in unfamiliar movement situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can practise and apply leadership, collaboration and group decision-making in physical activities (AC9HP8M09). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to the metacognitive skill of deliberately transferring movement skills and strategies from known to unknown contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students transfer and adapt movement skills and strategies from previous experiences to create successful outcomes in unfamiliar movement situations.

nodes.label: Identifying transferable skills and strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify which skills and strategies from previous movement experiences are likely to transfer to an unfamiliar situation
criteria: Names a specific skill or strategy from a familiar movement context
Identifies which elements transfer and explains the underlying principle that makes them transferable
Distinguishes between what transfers directly and what would need adaptation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify what is transferable and why cannot deliberately apply transfer in Node 2 — they will act intuitively rather than strategically, and the evaluation of transfer success in Node 2 requires having predicted what would transfer first.

width.minimum: Identify at least one skill or strategy from a familiar movement context and explain which elements are likely to transfer to a named unfamiliar situation
width.typical: Draw parallels between successful movement strategies in one sporting situation and how similar strategies could be used in a different sport; speculate on possible outcomes of innovative solutions based on past experience in outdoor or nature-based activities; identify which prior movement experiences are most relevant to a new challenge
wider: Systematically map transferable skills across two or more sport or movement contexts — identify what transfers directly, what needs adaptation, and what is genuinely new
Apply transfer thinking to an outdoor adventure activity (rope climbing, bushwalking, abseiling, kayaking) — identify which prior movement experiences are most relevant and why
Evaluate which aspects of a movement strategy are context-independent (transferable) versus context-specific (non-transferable) — build a framework for deciding what to transfer

modes.reason: Transfer thinking requires explicit reasoning about what makes a skill or strategy portable — what are the underlying principles that apply across contexts, versus what is specific to the original context. Students who move to unfamiliar situations without this reasoning just try familiar things without knowing why. The structured reasoning investment is in building the transfer analysis: what is the skill, what principle underpins it, in what other contexts does that principle apply.

nodes.label: Applying and evaluating transfer
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply transferred skills and strategies in unfamiliar situations and evaluate the success of the transfer
criteria: Attempts to apply a transferred skill or strategy in a named unfamiliar situation
Evaluates whether the transfer was successful — with specific reference to the outcome
Identifies what adaptation was needed and explains why the original form didn't transfer directly

width.minimum: Apply at least one transferred skill or strategy in an unfamiliar movement situation; evaluate whether the transfer was successful and what adaptation was needed
width.typical: Attempt innovative solutions to movement challenges in unfamiliar situations based on past experience; reflect on the effectiveness of movement solutions and suggest improvements; propose how the solution can be transferred to other movement situations
wider: Apply transfer across multiple unfamiliar situations — compare which transfers worked better and build explanations for why some transfers succeed more readily than others
Evaluate a failed transfer attempt — identify what was assumed to transfer that didn't, and explain why; propose what would need to be different for the transfer to succeed
Lead a group through an unfamiliar movement challenge by deliberately applying and teaching transfer thinking — evaluate the group's success and your own leadership of the transfer process

modes.reason: Transfer capability builds through repeated practice of the transfer cycle across multiple unfamiliar situations. A single successful transfer does not develop the metacognitive skill — students need to experience both successful and unsuccessful transfers, and to reflect on what determined the outcome. The elaborations explicitly require reflection on effectiveness and proposals for further transfer.

descriptors.title: Fair play and ethical behaviour
descriptors.description: demonstrate fair play and reflect on how ethical behaviour can influence physical activity outcomes for individuals and groups
descriptors.knowledge: Students can transfer and adapt skills from previous experiences to create successful outcomes in unfamiliar situations (AC9HP10M07), and have previously investigated modifications to equipment and rules supporting fair play and inclusion (AC9HP8M08). At Y9-10 the focus extends to reflecting on how ethical behaviour influences outcomes — including contested issues like performance-enhancing drugs.
descriptors.endpoint: Students demonstrate fair play and reflect on how ethical behaviour influences physical activity outcomes for individuals and groups, including engagement with contested ethical questions in sport.

nodes.label: Fair play in practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate fair play and analyse how equitable participation influences physical activity outcomes
criteria: Demonstrates at least one specific fair play behaviour during a physical activity
Identifies how equitable participation influenced the outcome — for themselves or others
Does not conflate rule-following with fair play — recognises that fair play includes spirit and intent

width.minimum: Demonstrate fair play in a physical activity context; identify one way equitable participation influenced the outcome for the group
width.typical: Demonstrate fair play across a range of physical activity contexts; analyse how equitable participation in group activities influences outcomes; analyse how First Nations Australian athletes have been treated in different sports and evaluate the impact on young First Nations Australians' participation
wider: Analyse a specific case of inequitable treatment in sport — evaluate what the impact was on participation, identity and outcomes for those affected, and for the broader sporting community
Investigate how First Nations Australian athletes have navigated inequitable treatment in sport — evaluate how their responses modelled ethical behaviour and influenced cultural change
Evaluate how equitable participation rules in a modified game affect the quality of the experience for all participants — redesign one element to improve equity and evaluate the impact

modes.reason: Fair play operates differently across individual sport, team sport, recreational activity, and elite competition contexts. Students who only demonstrate fair play in one familiar context develop a narrow understanding. The First Nations athlete direction is not optional — it addresses a substantive and historically significant dimension of fair play in Australian sport.

nodes.label: Ethical behaviour and sporting outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how ethical behaviour influences physical activity outcomes for individuals and groups, including engagement with contested ethical issues
criteria: Identifies a specific ethical issue and at least two competing positions on it
Reflects on how different ethical positions influence outcomes — not just which position is correct
Reasoning engages with evidence or principle — not only personal preference

width.minimum: Identify one contested ethical issue in sport and reflect on how different positions on it could influence outcomes for individuals and groups
width.typical: Investigate the use of performance-enhancing drugs in sport and analyse tensions between competing positions on whether they should be permitted; discuss the role of organisations (Sports Integrity Australia, sporting tribunals, Australian Human Rights Commission, Court of Arbitration for Sport) in promoting fairness and ethical behaviour; reflect on how ethical behaviour influences both individual and group outcomes
wider: Construct an evidence-based argument for one position on performance-enhancing drugs in sport — evaluate the strongest counterargument and address it
Investigate the role of Sports Integrity Australia or a specific sporting tribunal in a named case — evaluate how the resolution influenced ethical behaviour standards in that sport
Reflect on a personal experience where ethical or unethical behaviour influenced an outcome — evaluate what the experience revealed about the relationship between integrity and performance

modes.reason: Students commonly express strong opinions about ethical issues in sport (PEDs, racism, unfair treatment) without engaging the complexity — taking a position without analysing competing perspectives or evaluating evidence. The structured reasoning investment is in developing the capacity to hold and examine multiple positions simultaneously before reaching a reflective conclusion about how ethics influences outcomes.

descriptors.title: Leadership and decision-making
descriptors.description: devise, implement and refine strategies for decision-making when working in groups or teams that demonstrate leadership and collaboration skills
descriptors.knowledge: Students can demonstrate fair play and reflect on how ethical behaviour influences outcomes (AC9HP10M08), and have previously practised and applied leadership, collaboration and group decision-making in physical activities (AC9HP8M09). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to devising, implementing and refining decision-making strategies — a higher-order planning and evaluation task.
descriptors.endpoint: Students devise, implement and refine decision-making strategies for group and team contexts that demonstrate leadership and collaboration skills.

nodes.label: Devising decision-making strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can devise explicit strategies for group decision-making that demonstrate leadership and collaboration
criteria: Articulates a specific decision-making approach — not just 'we'll discuss it'
Strategy includes a mechanism for incorporating different perspectives or resolving disagreement
Explains how leadership is distributed — who decides what, and how
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot devise an explicit decision-making strategy cannot implement and refine one in Node 2 — refinement requires a concrete intended approach to evaluate against actual group outcomes.

width.minimum: Devise one strategy for making a group decision in a physical activity context; explain how it distributes leadership and incorporates different perspectives
width.typical: Devise decision-making strategies that incorporate leadership, collaboration and group dynamics; analyse leadership styles and group dynamics through initiative games; use self-talk and encouragement to motivate team members; evaluate their own contribution to teamwork and enjoyable participation
wider: Devise and implement a decision-making strategy for a complex group movement challenge — evaluate how the strategy performed under pressure and what adjustments were needed
Analyse different leadership styles (directive, collaborative, distributed) through initiative games — evaluate when each style is most effective and for which group composition
Design and implement self-assessment and peer-assessment tools to evaluate performance across multiple group roles — use findings to refine leadership approach

modes.reason: Students commonly lead groups without making their decision-making strategy explicit — acting on instinct without articulating the approach. The investment is in making the strategy explicit: how will decisions be made in this group, what is each person's role, how will disagreement be handled. This articulation is prerequisite for implementation and refinement.

nodes.label: Implementing and refining leadership strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can implement and refine decision-making strategies in group contexts, using assessment tools to evaluate and improve
criteria: Implements the devised strategy — not just describes it
Evaluates a specific aspect of how the strategy performed — what worked and what didn't
Identifies a concrete refinement based on the evaluation, not a generic improvement

width.minimum: Implement a devised decision-making strategy in a group activity; evaluate how well it worked and identify one specific refinement
width.typical: Implement and refine decision-making strategies across group and team contexts; use self-assessment and peer-assessment tools to evaluate performance in multiple roles; apply self-talk and encouragement to support persistence; evaluate their own contribution to teamwork quality and enjoyment for all
wider: Implement the same decision-making strategy across two different group contexts (e.g. different team sizes, different challenge types) and evaluate how the strategy needed to be adapted for each
Create a peer-assessment tool for evaluating leadership and collaboration; use it with a group member and use their feedback to refine your own leadership approach
Lead a group through an initiative problem and document the decision-making process in real time — evaluate the gap between the devised strategy and what actually happened, and propose refinements

modes.reason: Leadership and collaboration capability develops through implementing and refining strategies across multiple group contexts — different team sizes, different challenges, different group compositions. A single implementation does not produce transferable leadership capability. The assessment tools direction supports systematic reflection rather than impression-based evaluation.

descriptors.title: Factors shaping identities
descriptors.description: analyse factors that shape identities and evaluate how individuals influence the identities of others
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine how power, coercion and gender stereotypes influence roles and relationships (AC9HP8P03). They have not yet analysed the broader range of societal, cultural, and community factors that shape identity, nor evaluated how individuals actively influence each other's identities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse multiple factors that shape identities — including societal norms, cultural practices, and community belonging — and evaluate how individuals influence the identities of others.

nodes.label: Societal and cultural factors on identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how societal norms, stereotypes and cultural practices shape how individuals see themselves
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct factors (e.g. societal norms, cultural practices, stereotypes) that shape identity
Explains how each factor operates in a specific context with reference to evidence or examples
Does not conflate identity with personality — recognises identity as socially and culturally shaped
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot analyse how external factors shape identity cannot meaningfully evaluate how individuals influence each other's identities in Node 2 — that evaluative move requires a working understanding of which forces are already at play before individual influence is layered on top.

width.minimum: Identify at least two societal or cultural factors that influence identity and explain how each shapes self-perception in a specific context
width.typical: Analyse how societal norms, stereotypes and cultural expectations influence how young people view themselves across multiple contexts (e.g. school, sport, online); evaluate which factors are most influential and why
wider: Analyse how personal totems in First Nations Australian cultures contribute to individual identity, comparing this with how identity markers function in other cultural traditions

Investigate how cultural beliefs and practices surrounding transitions to adulthood differ across cultures, including cultures of Asia, and what this reveals about how identity is constructed differently across communities
Examine how societal norms and stereotypes specifically influence perceptions of movement competence, and how this shapes participation and identity in physical activity contexts

modes.reason: Identity is shaped differently across contexts — what norms operate in sport differ from those online or within family. Students need multiple distinct contexts to develop the analytical skill rather than a single worked example. First Nations and Asian cultural contexts are not optional extras; they are substantive different frameworks for understanding how identity is constructed.

nodes.label: Individuals influencing others' identities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how individuals — including family, friends and community — actively influence the identities of others
criteria: Identifies a specific individual or group (family, friend, community) and names their influence on another's identity
Evaluates whether the influence is enabling, constraining, or both, with reasoning
Proposes at least one strategy for enhancing positive identity influence

width.minimum: Describe one way in which family, friends or community influence another person's identity; evaluate whether that influence is positive, limiting, or both
width.typical: Analyse the role of family, friends and community in supporting an individual's identity; evaluate strategies that could enhance their own and others' wellbeing by strengthening positive identity influences
wider: Investigate how changing social standing within First Nations Australian communities alters the roles individuals play in shaping community identity — and how this differs from Western individualist models of influence

Propose and evaluate specific strategies for how a peer, family member or community figure could actively support the positive identity development of a young person navigating competing societal expectations

Examine how movement and physical activity contexts can be deliberately structured to influence participants' identity — e.g. how a coach or team culture shapes whether someone sees themselves as an athlete

modes.reason: Students often describe influence without evaluating it — naming that parents influence identity without assessing whether that influence is enabling or constraining. Scaffolding the evaluative move explicitly (what is the influence, in what direction does it operate, what are its effects on wellbeing, what would a positive alternative look like) helps students reach the evaluative claim the descriptor requires.

descriptors.title: Managing changes and transitions
descriptors.description: refine, evaluate and adapt strategies for managing changes and transitions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse factors that shape identities and evaluate how individuals influence others' identities (AC9HP10P01). They have previously investigated resources and strategies to manage changes including puberty (AC9HP6P02) and analysed the impact of changes and transitions (AC9HP8P02). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to refining, evaluating and adapting — not introducing strategies for the first time.
descriptors.endpoint: Students refine, evaluate and adapt strategies for managing changes and transitions, including asserting their stance respectfully and responding to changing social and behavioural expectations.

nodes.label: Evaluating existing strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of strategies they have previously used or learned for managing changes and transitions
criteria: Names a specific strategy for managing a change or transition
Evaluates its effectiveness with reference to a specific situation or context
Identifies at least one condition under which the strategy works well and one where it is less effective
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate the effectiveness of strategies cannot meaningfully refine or adapt them in Node 2 — refinement requires a prior evaluative judgement about what needs to change and why.

width.minimum: Identify one strategy for managing a change or transition and evaluate its effectiveness in a specific situation — what worked, what didn't, and why
width.typical: Assess behavioural expectations across different relationships and social situations; evaluate how these expectations influence decisions and actions when managing transitions; identify which strategies are most effective for different types of change
wider: Analyse how changing roles and responsibilities for First Nations Australians as social standing changes within communities creates distinct transition challenges — evaluate what strategies are culturally appropriate versus imposed from outside
Investigate the impact of border crossing on identity and transition for First Nations Australians, evaluating the specific strategies needed when navigating between cultural contexts

Evaluate strategies for managing digital transitions (e.g. changing social media presence, online identity shifts) as a distinct category of contemporary transition that existing frameworks may not fully address

modes.reason: Students often describe strategies without evaluating them — listing what they would do without assessing whether it works or why. Scaffolding the evaluative move (what was the strategy, in what context, what was the outcome, what does this reveal about when it works) is the key investment here. The First Nations transition contexts require particular care — evaluation must include cultural appropriateness as a criterion, not just effectiveness by generic measures.

nodes.label: Refining and adapting strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine and adapt strategies for managing changes and transitions, including asserting their position respectfully in challenging situations
criteria: Demonstrates a refined or adapted strategy for a specific transition situation
Explains what was changed from a prior approach and the reasoning for the change
Rehearsed strategy includes acknowledgement of others' perspectives or feelings, not only self-assertion

width.minimum: Rehearse one refined strategy for managing a challenging transition situation; explain what was adapted from a prior approach and why
width.typical: Practise skills for dealing with challenging or unsafe situations (refusal skills, communicating choices, expressing opinions, contingency plans); rehearse asserting a stance on a dilemma by expressing thoughts and beliefs while acknowledging others' feelings; evaluate which adapted strategies are most effective
