wider: Design and rehearse a strategy for asserting a position in a culturally complex transition — e.g. navigating between community and family expectations and individual identity needs

Practise refusal skills and contingency planning for situations involving peer pressure around risk-taking (substance use, unsafe situations), evaluating which communication approaches are most effective in which social contexts
Evaluate how the same adaptive strategy performs differently in face-to-face versus online transition contexts and propose modifications for each

modes.reason: Refining and adapting strategies is a capability that builds through practising a range of situations. A single rehearsed scenario is insufficient — students need to build a repertoire of adapted responses across different transition types (social, cultural, online, risk-related) so that the adaptation skill itself becomes flexible. The elaborations explicitly require rehearsal across multiple scenario types.

descriptors.title: Gender equality and violence prevention
descriptors.description: investigate how gender equality and challenging assumptions about gender can prevent violence and abuse in relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can refine, evaluate and adapt strategies for managing changes and transitions (AC9HP10P02), and have previously examined how power, coercion and gender stereotypes influence roles and relationships (AC9HP8P03). At Y9-10, the focus moves from examining influence to investigating the causal link between gender assumptions and violence prevention.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how gender equality and challenging gender assumptions can prevent violence and abuse in relationships, including analysing attitudes that excuse or condone gender-based violence and evaluating how equality empowers respectful relationships.

nodes.label: Attitudes that enable gender-based violence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how attitudes towards gender equality and power lead to practices of coercion, harassment and violence
criteria: Names at least two specific attitudes or beliefs linked to gender-based violence
Explains how each attitude translates into harmful behaviour — not just that it does, but how
Does not conflate gender-based violence with all relationship conflict — recognises the specific role of power and gender norms
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot analyse how specific attitudes enable violence cannot make the causal argument in Node 2 — that challenging those attitudes prevents violence. The prevention argument depends entirely on having established the enabling mechanism first.

width.minimum: Identify at least two attitudes or beliefs that can lead to gender-based violence; explain the mechanism — how does holding that attitude translate into harmful behaviour
width.typical: Analyse how attitudes towards gender equality and power affect expectations and behaviour, leading to practices of sexual coercion, harassment, violence and submission; investigate and challenge specific attitudes that lead people to enact, excuse or condone gender-based violence
wider: Explore scenarios in texts demonstrating how gender inequality arises from intergenerational patterns of inequity and unequal power, and analyse what makes these patterns self-reinforcing
Investigate how media representations normalise or challenge attitudes that condone gender-based violence — evaluate a specific example using evidence
Analyse how the same attitudes play out differently in online versus offline relationships, and what this means for prevention strategies

modes.reason: Students often assert that certain attitudes are wrong without analysing the mechanism by which they enable harm. The key investment is scaffolding the causal reasoning: what is the attitude, who holds it, in what context does it operate, how does it translate into specific harmful behaviours. Without this chain the prevention argument in Node 2 has no foundation.

nodes.label: Gender equality as prevention
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how gender equality and challenging gender assumptions can prevent violence and empower respectful relationships
criteria: Explains a specific causal link between gender equality and reduced violence or coercion
Proposes at least one concrete strategy for challenging gender inequality in a named community context
Reasoning goes beyond assertion — includes evidence, mechanism, or condition under which the strategy works

width.minimum: Explain one way in which greater gender equality reduces the conditions that enable violence or coercion in relationships
width.typical: Evaluate how gender equality empowers people to develop equal and respectful relationships; propose strategies for challenging gender inequality in their own communities; examine intergenerational patterns of inequity and propose community-level prevention responses
wider: Design and evaluate a community strategy for challenging a specific gender inequality that contributes to relationship violence in a local context
Investigate how First Nations communities have developed gender equity approaches that reflect cultural sovereignty — evaluate how these differ from and complement mainstream prevention frameworks
Evaluate the evidence for bystander intervention programs as a gender equality strategy: what do they change, for whom, and under what conditions

modes.reason: Students commonly make the claim that equality prevents violence without evaluating the causal logic. Scaffolding the evaluative argument (if this inequality creates this condition for violence, then reducing this inequality disrupts this condition in this way) is the key teaching investment. The wider directions — First Nations approaches, bystander programs — each require this same evaluative structure applied to a different prevention model.

descriptors.title: Evaluating respectful relationships
descriptors.description: evaluate the influence of respect, empathy, power and coercion on establishing and maintaining respectful relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain and apply skills to communicate assertively when seeking, giving or denying consent (AC9HP8P07). They have previously examined roles of respect, empathy, power and coercion in respectful relationships (AC9HP8P04). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to evaluation — assessing how these factors operate and what happens when the balance shifts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate how respect, empathy, power and coercion influence whether relationships are established and maintained as respectful, including the influence of historical inequity and the forms violence can take.

nodes.label: Power and coercion in relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how power imbalances and coercion undermine respectful relationships
criteria: Identifies a specific power imbalance and explains how it operates in a relationship
Evaluates the effect on at least one party's autonomy, rights or wellbeing
Proposes a specific action that could be taken when a relationship becomes coercive or disrespectful
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate how power imbalances operate cannot assess the role of respect and empathy as countervailing forces in Node 2 — the constructive analysis requires first having established where and how coercion undermines relationships.

width.minimum: Identify a power imbalance in a relationship scenario and evaluate how it affects the ability of both parties to maintain respect and autonomy
width.typical: Investigate how the balance of power influences the nature of relationships; evaluate the characteristics of positive, respectful relationships against the rights and ethical responsibilities of individuals; propose actions when a relationship is not respectful
wider: Investigate how historical patterns of inequity, violence and discrimination have lasting intergenerational effects on wellbeing — evaluate strategies for building cultural awareness and empathy that contribute to reconciliation

Analyse how bullying, racism and gender-based violence take different forms (verbal, physical, emotional, sexual, economic) in face-to-face and online environments — evaluate which forms are most commonly underrecognised and why
Investigate how demonstrating support for truth-telling causes can build cultural awareness, empathy and more respectful relationships at community level

modes.reason: Students often name that power imbalances are harmful without evaluating how they operate — the mechanism by which coercion undermines respect and autonomy. The structured reasoning investment is in building the evaluative chain: what power imbalance, in what relationship context, what effect on each party's rights, what does a respectful response look like. The intergenerational inequity direction requires this same chain applied at a historical and cultural scale.

nodes.label: Respect and empathy as relational foundations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how respect and empathy actively establish and maintain respectful relationships
criteria: Identifies specific behaviours or practices that demonstrate respect or empathy in a relationship
Evaluates what respect or empathy requires from each party — not just what it looks like from outside
Distinguishes between genuine respect/empathy and performative compliance

width.minimum: Explain one way in which demonstrating respect or empathy strengthens a relationship; evaluate what this requires from each party
width.typical: Evaluate the rights and ethical responsibilities of individuals in relationships; investigate the characteristics of positive, respectful relationships; propose and evaluate actions that build respect and empathy across different relationship types
wider: Evaluate how public acknowledgement of cultural contributions (e.g. First Nations Australians in sport and community) functions as a form of respect that builds relational trust at community level — not just in individual relationships
Design a scenario-based evaluation tool that assesses whether a relationship demonstrates respect, empathy and equitable power — apply it to at least two different relationship types
Investigate how cultural practices of empathy and respect differ across communities and evaluate what this means for respectful cross-cultural relationships

modes.reason: Respect and empathy operate differently across relationship types — peer, romantic, family, online, cross-cultural. Students who only evaluate these in one relationship context develop a narrow understanding that may not transfer. Working across multiple relationship types and cultural contexts builds a more generalisable evaluative capability.

descriptors.title: Challenging bias and promoting inclusion
descriptors.description: propose strategies and actions individuals and groups can implement to challenge biases, stereotypes, prejudices and discrimination, and promote inclusion in their communities
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate the influence of respect, empathy, power and coercion on respectful relationships (AC9HP10P04), and have previously investigated strategies that influence how communities value diversity (AC9HP8P05). At Y9-10 the focus moves to proposing and designing concrete strategies and actions for challenging bias and discrimination.
descriptors.endpoint: Students propose and evaluate specific strategies and actions for challenging biases, stereotypes, prejudices and discrimination, and for promoting inclusion in their communities.

nodes.label: Analysing bias and discrimination
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how prejudice, marginalisation and discrimination operate and their implications for individuals and communities
criteria: Names a specific form of bias or discrimination and identifies who is affected
Analyses the mechanism — how does this bias operate, not just that it causes harm
Distinguishes between individual prejudice and systemic discrimination
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot analyse how specific forms of bias operate cannot propose targeted strategies to counter them in Node 2 — effective strategies require understanding the mechanism of the bias, not just naming that it exists.

width.minimum: Identify one form of bias or discrimination (e.g. homophobia, racism, gender stereotyping) and analyse its implications for a targeted individual or group
width.typical: Analyse the implications of prejudice, marginalisation, homophobia, racism, discrimination, violence and harassment on individuals and communities; critique media representations of cultural and racial groups for whether they are respectful, realistic and inclusive; analyse gender norm messaging in popular culture and evaluate its impact
wider: Investigate community health resources and evaluate how accessible they are for marginalised individuals and groups — propose specific changes to improve inclusiveness and accessibility
Analyse how biases and discrimination targeting specific cultural groups, including Australians of Asian heritage, operate and what community-level countermeasures exist

Critique a specific media representation of a First Nations Australian community — evaluate whether it is respectful, realistic and inclusive, and what its likely impact is on community members' identities and wellbeing

modes.reason: Different forms of bias and discrimination operate through different mechanisms and affect different communities in different ways. Homophobia, racism, and gender stereotyping are not interchangeable — each requires distinct analysis. Students need to develop analytical capability across multiple forms of bias, not deep expertise in one. The First Nations and Asian heritage directions are not optional — they are substantive different analytical contexts.

nodes.label: Proposing inclusion strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose specific strategies and actions that individuals and groups can implement to challenge bias and promote inclusion
criteria: Proposes a specific strategy linked to a named form of bias or discrimination
Explains how the strategy addresses the mechanism of the bias — not just that it opposes it
Identifies at least one condition or barrier that could affect the strategy's effectiveness

width.minimum: Propose one strategy for challenging a specific form of bias or discrimination and explain how it addresses the mechanism identified in analysis
width.typical: Design strategies and actions to challenge stereotypes, prejudices and discrimination; propose countermeasures against specific harmful behaviours; publicly acknowledge contributions of First Nations Australians to Australian sporting and health fields as a concrete inclusion action; propose strategies to challenge biases targeting Australians of Asian heritage
wider: Investigate a community-action initiative led by young people that promotes inclusion and evaluate what made it effective — what could be replicated in a school or local context
Design a multi-level strategy (individual, group, institutional) for promoting inclusion in a specific community context, evaluating what each level can and cannot achieve alone
Evaluate bystander intervention as an inclusion strategy — under what conditions does it work, what barriers exist, and how can those barriers be reduced for a specific school or community context

modes.reason: Students commonly propose generic strategies (be kind, raise awareness) without connecting them to the specific mechanism of the bias. The key investment is building the reasoning chain: this bias operates through this mechanism, therefore this strategy disrupts it at this point. Strategies that do not address the mechanism are unlikely to be effective, and the evaluation criterion requires more than good intentions.

descriptors.title: Evaluating emotional responses
descriptors.description: evaluate emotional responses in different situations to refine strategies for managing emotions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can propose strategies to challenge biases and promote inclusion (AC9HP10P05), and have previously analysed factors that influence emotional responses and devised self-management strategies (AC9HP8P06). At Y9-10 the focus shifts from devising strategies to evaluating emotional responses and refining existing strategies based on that evaluation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate emotional responses in different situations — including extreme or uncontrolled responses — and use that evaluation to refine strategies for managing emotions.

nodes.label: Evaluating emotional responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the consequences of emotional responses — their own and others' — in a range of situations
criteria: Identifies a specific emotional response in a specific situation
Evaluates the consequence of that response for the situation and for at least one relationship
Distinguishes between the emotion itself and the behavioural response — recognises both are relevant to evaluation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate emotional responses — what triggered them, what effects they had, what alternative responses were available — cannot refine strategies in Node 2. Strategy refinement requires prior evaluative judgement about what the current response achieved and what it failed to achieve.

width.minimum: Describe one situation where an emotional response (their own or observed) had a significant impact — evaluate what the response was, why it occurred, and what effect it had
width.typical: Reflect on the possible consequences of not recognising emotions in challenging situations including rejection, failure, harassment and violence; evaluate situations where extreme or uncontrolled emotion occurs and its impact on the situation and relationships; analyse how others might be affected by their own emotional responses
wider: Evaluate a case study of conflict escalation — trace the emotional responses at each stage and evaluate where a different response could have changed the outcome
Analyse emotional responses in online environments (e.g. responding to harassment, rejection or exclusion online) and evaluate whether strategies that work face-to-face transfer effectively
Evaluate the consequences of emotional responses in physical activity contexts — how does uncontrolled emotion (frustration, aggression) affect team dynamics, fair play and individual performance

modes.reason: Students commonly describe emotional responses without evaluating them — narrating what happened without assessing the consequence chain. The structured reasoning investment is in building the evaluative sequence: what was the emotional response, what triggered it, what was its effect on the situation, on relationships, on the person themselves. This evaluation is prerequisite for the refinement work in Node 2.

nodes.label: Refining emotion management strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine strategies for managing emotions based on evaluation of past responses
criteria: Identifies a specific refinement to an existing strategy with reasoning for the change
Refined strategy is applicable to a named situation type — not only described in the abstract
Evaluates what the refined strategy improves compared to the prior approach

width.minimum: Identify one strategy they have previously used for managing emotions and explain what refinement would improve its effectiveness based on evaluation
width.typical: Propose refined strategies for managing emotional responses and resolving conflict across family, school, social and online environments; evaluate which refined strategies are most effective in which contexts and why
wider: Develop and rehearse a refined strategy for a specific high-stakes emotional situation (e.g. receiving criticism, experiencing rejection, witnessing injustice) — evaluate its effectiveness through peer feedback or reflection
Design an emotion regulation framework for a physical activity or team sport context that addresses the specific emotional challenges of competition, failure and group dynamics
Evaluate how cultural norms about emotional expression affect which strategies are available and effective — propose adaptations for cross-cultural or diverse community contexts

modes.reason: Refined emotion management requires a repertoire of strategies across different contexts — what works in a family conflict may not work under competitive pressure or in an online exchange. Building range across situation types is more valuable than perfecting a single strategy. The elaborations explicitly require strategies across family, school, social and online environments.

descriptors.title: Consent and respectful relationships
descriptors.description: examine how strategies, such as communicating choices, seeking, giving and denying consent, and expressing opinions and needs can support the development of respectful relationships, including sexual relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate emotional responses and refine emotion management strategies (AC9HP10P06), and have previously explained and applied assertive consent communication skills (AC9HP8P07). At Y9-10 the focus expands to examining how consent communication strategies support the development of respectful relationships broadly, including sexual relationships.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how communicating choices, seeking, giving and denying consent, and expressing opinions and needs support respectful relationships, including understanding legal requirements and the importance of taking responsibility for their own actions.

nodes.label: Consent communication strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and refine strategies for communicating consent clearly and respectfully across a range of relationship scenarios
criteria: Describes at least one specific consent communication strategy with reference to a named scenario type
Strategy includes both verbal and non-verbal components, or explicitly addresses what to do when non-verbal cues are absent
Reflects on taking responsibility for own behaviour — not only on what others should do
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot articulate and refine specific consent communication strategies cannot examine their relationship-building function in Node 2 — the examination of how strategies support relationships requires first having identified what those strategies actually are.

width.minimum: Describe one strategy for communicating consent clearly in a specific relationship scenario; explain what makes it effective
width.typical: Refine strategies for communicating choices, needs and opinions clearly and respectfully across peer group, family and work situations; describe strategies that enhance safety and wellbeing of sexual partners including communicating feelings, respecting boundaries, gaining affirmative consent, and assertive communication; reflect on taking responsibility for own actions
wider: Investigate the legal requirements for consent in your state or territory — including seeking, giving, refusing and accepting refusal in online and offline interactions with friends, colleagues, strangers and intimate partners — and evaluate how these laws connect to respectful relationship principles
Rehearse consent communication in scenarios where social pressure or power imbalances are present — evaluate which strategies are most effective and why
Examine how consent communication strategies need to adapt for digital contexts (texting, social media, online relationships) where verbal and non-verbal cues are absent

modes.reason: Consent communication is a capability that requires a repertoire across relationship types and contexts. Peer group, family, intimate partner, and online contexts each require different communication approaches. The legal dimension (state/territory requirements) adds a factual layer that students need alongside the skills dimension. Building range across contexts is more valuable than polishing a single scenario response.

nodes.label: Consent supporting respectful relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how consent communication strategies support the development of respectful relationships, including sexual relationships
criteria: Explains a specific connection between practising consent communication and a quality of the relationship it builds
Includes sexual relationships as one context — does not treat consent as relevant only to intimate relationships
Reflects on own responsibility — not only on what makes a relationship respectful in the abstract

width.minimum: Explain one way in which practising consent communication supports the development of a more respectful relationship
width.typical: Examine how strategies for communicating choices, seeking and denying consent, and expressing needs support respectful relationships broadly and sexual relationships specifically; reflect on potential impact of own behaviour on others; examine how consent communication connects to affirmative consent, individual rights, and mutual respect
wider: Examine how the portrayal of consent in TV shows, movies, popular music and online content may influence people's beliefs about what respectful and consensual relationships look like — evaluate the gap between media representations and legal/ethical standards

Investigate how consent and respectful communication functions differently in relationships where power is unequal (e.g. age gaps, social status, online anonymity) and evaluate what additional strategies are needed
Design a peer education resource on consent for a specific audience (e.g. Year 8 students, parents/carers) — evaluate what framing and examples would be most effective

modes.reason: This node integrates consent communication skills (Node 1) with the broader relationship development framework — showing how practising consent is not a procedural compliance exercise but is constitutive of respectful relationships. Students who can communicate consent but cannot explain its relational function have not reached the descriptor's command term. The integration task is connecting the skill to the relationship quality it produces.

descriptors.title: Managing health risk situations
descriptors.description: plan, rehearse and evaluate strategies for managing situations where their own or others' health, safety or wellbeing may be at risk
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and implement strategies using health resources to enhance health, safety and wellbeing (AC9HP8P10). At Y9-10 the focus moves to more complex risk situations — peer pressure around substance use, first aid including CPR, consent under impairment, and safe blood practices — with evaluation of strategies added to planning and rehearsal.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, rehearse and evaluate strategies for managing health and safety risk situations, including peer pressure, first aid emergencies, digital safety, and safe practices in a range of risk contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying and planning for risk situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify health risk situations and plan realistic strategies for managing them
criteria: Names a specific health risk situation and identifies who may be at risk
Plans a realistic response strategy — not an idealised one that ignores social or contextual constraints
Plan includes at least one external resource or support service that could be accessed
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot plan realistic strategies for named risk situations cannot rehearse and evaluate them in Node 2 — rehearsal requires a concrete plan to enact and evaluate.

width.minimum: Identify one health risk situation (e.g. peer pressure, emergency, digital safety risk) and plan a realistic response strategy
width.typical: Identify a range of health risk situations relevant to young people; plan realistic responses including refusal skills, communicating choices, contingency plans; critique the appropriateness and effectiveness of support services available in the local community for young people
wider: Plan responses to scenarios involving peer pressure around e-cigarettes, cannabis, psychostimulants, opiates or hallucinogens — evaluate which refusal strategies are most realistic in peer group social contexts

Investigate safe blood practices across a range of situations (not sharing needles, precautions in physical activity, safe sexual practices including use of condoms and dams) and plan how to raise these practices with peers in an accessible way

Examine factors that impact ability to seek, give or deny consent when a person is affected by alcohol or other drugs, or where there is a power imbalance — plan strategies for recognising and responding to these situations

modes.reason: Health risk situations are diverse — peer pressure around substances, physical emergencies, digital safety, and consent under impairment each require different strategies. Students need to plan across multiple risk types rather than developing one polished response. The elaborations explicitly require multiple risk contexts.

nodes.label: Rehearsing and evaluating risk responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can rehearse and evaluate strategies for managing health risk situations, including first aid responses
criteria: Rehearses a strategy for at least one named risk situation
Evaluates its effectiveness — identifies what worked, what was difficult, and what would be changed
Evaluation is specific to the scenario context, not generic ('it went well')

width.minimum: Rehearse one strategy for a health risk situation and evaluate its effectiveness — what worked, what barriers emerged, what would be done differently
width.typical: Rehearse responses to a range of risk scenarios including peer pressure situations and first aid emergencies (including CPR); evaluate the appropriateness and effectiveness of responses; investigate behaviours that constitute safe, legal and ethical conduct in digital environments and identify actions to take when behaviour becomes abusive
wider: Practise and evaluate CPR and basic first aid responses — evaluate own performance against criteria and identify what further practice is needed
Rehearse a range of realistic refusal skill scenarios (substance offers, unsafe situations) and evaluate which verbal and non-verbal strategies are most effective across different social contexts
Evaluate available digital safety resources and support services for young people — assess which are most accessible and effective for specific risk situations young people in your community face

modes.reason: Rehearsal across multiple risk scenario types builds a repertoire of response strategies that can be accessed in real situations. A single rehearsed response is insufficient — the elaborations explicitly require rehearsal across peer pressure scenarios, first aid emergencies, and digital safety situations. The evaluation component requires students to assess effectiveness, not just complete the rehearsal.

descriptors.title: Critique health information and media
descriptors.description: critique health information, services and media messaging about relationships, lifestyle choices, health decisions and behaviours to evaluate their influence on individual attitudes and actions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, rehearse and evaluate strategies for managing health and safety risk situations (AC9HP10P08), and have previously investigated how media and influential people impact health attitudes and behaviours (AC9HP8P09). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to critique — a higher-order evaluative move that assesses the validity, bias and influence of health information and media.
descriptors.endpoint: Students critique health information, services and media messaging to evaluate their influence on attitudes and actions across relationships, lifestyle choices, health decisions and health behaviours.

nodes.label: Criteria for critiquing health information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify criteria for evaluating the quality, bias and influence of health information and media messaging
criteria: Names at least two criteria for evaluating health information quality or bias
Applies criteria to a specific example — not just describes them in the abstract
Criteria include something beyond 'is from a reliable source' — e.g. considers whose interests are served, what is left out, who the audience is
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify criteria for evaluating health information cannot apply critique in Node 2 — critique requires a principled basis, not just personal opinion about whether information seems right.

width.minimum: Identify at least two criteria for evaluating health information (e.g. source credibility, evidence base, whose interests are served) and apply them to one example
width.typical: Develop criteria for critiquing health information and services; apply criteria to evaluate health information targeting specific groups of young people (substance use, healthy food choices, fitness plans, mental health support, sexual health, personal safety); evaluate strategies and actions to increase personal safety
wider: Analyse the nutritional composition of foods eaten by First Peoples of Australia and evaluate how this information could be used to increase health benefits for everyone — assess how this knowledge has been presented in mainstream health media

Investigate health issues specific to First Nations Australian communities and critique mainstream health messaging for its relevance and accessibility — propose proactive community strategies for promoting better access and health outcomes

Critique health information targeting specific cultural or demographic groups (e.g. young men, LGBTIQ+ youth, culturally and linguistically diverse communities) — evaluate whether the information addresses actual barriers to health access

modes.reason: Students commonly express opinions about health information without applying evaluative criteria — saying a source is unreliable without specifying why by what standard. The investment is in building the criteria explicitly first: what makes health information credible, what indicates bias, what does it mean to evaluate whose interests a message serves. These criteria then underpin the critique work in Node 2.

nodes.label: Critiquing media messaging about health
nodes.checkpoint: Students can critique health information and media messaging to evaluate their influence on attitudes and actions
criteria: Applies specific criteria (from Node 1) to critique a named piece of health information or media
Evaluates the likely influence on attitudes or actions — not just the quality of the information itself
Identifies what is absent or distorted in the message, not only what it gets wrong

width.minimum: Critique one piece of health information or media messaging — apply criteria to evaluate its quality, identify its likely influence on attitudes, and explain what it leaves out
width.typical: Critique health information and services across multiple domains (substance use, food, fitness, mental health, sexual health, personal safety); critique how the portrayal of sexual relationships in TV, advertisements, movies, popular music and online content may influence beliefs about respectful, safe and consensual relationships; evaluate influence on individual attitudes and actions
wider: Critique a specific media portrayal of sexual relationships (film, TV, pornography, advertising) using evidence-based criteria for respectful and consensual relationships — evaluate the gap between the portrayal and legal/ethical standards
Investigate and critique a health campaign targeting a specific community — evaluate whether it is culturally appropriate, accessible, and likely to achieve its stated goals
Design a counter-messaging strategy for a specific piece of misleading health information — evaluate what approach would most effectively reach the target audience

modes.reason: Health media critique requires practice across different domains and message types — food advertising operates differently from sexual health messaging in social media, which operates differently from a government health campaign. Students need to apply their criteria across multiple message types to develop genuine critique capability. The sexual relationships media direction is particularly important given the elaborations' explicit inclusion of pornography and its influence on consent beliefs.

descriptors.title: Plan and critique health strategies
descriptors.description: plan, justify and critique strategies to enhance their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing
descriptors.knowledge: Students can critique health information and media messaging to evaluate their influence on attitudes and actions (AC9HP10P09). At Y9-10 this standard integrates critique capability with strategy planning and justification — moving from evaluating others' messages to designing and critically assessing their own strategies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan, justify and critique strategies to enhance health, safety, relationships and wellbeing — across individual, community and cultural dimensions, including mental health and wellbeing strategies.

nodes.label: Planning and justifying health strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a strategy to enhance health, safety, relationships or wellbeing and justify it with evidence and reasoning
criteria: Plans a specific strategy with a named health or wellbeing outcome
Justification includes at least one reason drawn from evidence, theory or prior experience — not only personal preference
Strategy is realistic — acknowledges at least one constraint or barrier to implementation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot plan and justify a strategy cannot then critique it in Node 2 — critique of a strategy requires first having a concrete strategy to evaluate and a justification to interrogate.

width.minimum: Plan one strategy for enhancing a specific health or wellbeing outcome; justify the approach with at least one piece of evidence or reasoning about why it will be effective
width.typical: Plan and justify strategies across individual and community levels; consider social, cultural and economic factors that may influence health behaviours and help-seeking; design strategies that enhance mental health and wellbeing (regular physical activity, positive self-talk, sleep habits, mindfulness, social connection); investigate community-action initiatives and evaluate what made them effective
wider: Plan a strategy for sustainable food practices — justify its health, environmental and community benefits; evaluate whether it is accessible and realistic for the target community

Engage with nature-based health activities and plan a strategy for incorporating them; explore how a deep connection to Country/Place enhances health and wellbeing for First Nations Australians and evaluate how this knowledge could inform mainstream health strategy planning

Investigate the pharmacopeia and health practices of First Nations Australian communities (with respect for ICIP protocols); evaluate how these practices could inform broader community health strategies while maintaining cultural integrity

modes.reason: Students commonly plan strategies without justifying them — describing what they would do without explaining why it will work or for whom. The justification move is critical here: what evidence supports this approach, what theory of change underpins it, what conditions does it require. This structured justification is also what makes the critique in Node 2 substantive rather than superficial.

nodes.label: Critiquing health strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can critique health strategies — their own and others' — for effectiveness, accessibility, and cultural appropriateness
criteria: Applies specific criteria to critique a health strategy — not just expresses a general opinion
Critique addresses accessibility — who can access this strategy and who cannot, and why
Proposes at least one concrete improvement, not only identifies what is wrong

width.minimum: Apply at least two criteria to critique a health strategy (their own or another's) — evaluate what it achieves, what it misses, and for whom it is most and least accessible
width.typical: Critique strategies for enhancing health, safety, relationships and wellbeing; analyse how social, cultural and economic factors influence the accessibility of strategies and help-seeking; evaluate the influence of stigma on access to health support (menstrual health, gender and sexual diversity, sexual health, mental illness); propose constructive improvements to online/digital health promotion strategies
wider: Investigate cultural rights of First Nations Australians to maintain traditional diets; critique how mainstream health strategies address or fail to address this right, and evaluate the proven health and wellbeing benefits
Critique an existing school or community health strategy against criteria including cultural appropriateness, accessibility, and evidence base — propose specific improvements

Evaluate how stigma associated with specific health issues (mental health, sexual health, menstrual health) affects help-seeking in your community — critique current strategies for reducing stigma and propose targeted improvements

modes.reason: This node integrates planning/justification (Node 1) with critique capability developed across P09 and P10 — students are now applying critical evaluation to strategies they have themselves designed or selected. The integration is between the planning perspective (what does this strategy aim to do) and the critical perspective (for whom does it work, what does it miss, what does it assume). This is the highest-order move in the P strand at this band.

Critique of health strategies requires application across different health domains and community contexts. Critiquing a mental health strategy requires different criteria than critiquing a food sustainability strategy or a First Nations traditional diet rights framework. Range across health domains builds genuine critique capability.
